lessons.title: Baseline and positioning: role families, JD decoding and your story
lessons.summary: Choose three AI role families, decode job descriptions into a gap tracker, baseline your skills with mocks, and build an honest transition story.
keyPoints: Think in role families by what the work is: Software Engineer AI, GenAI/LLM Engineer, AI Application Engineer, Agentic AI Engineer, and AI Platform/LLMOps as a stretch.
Pick at most three families: one primary, one adjacent, one stretch, each with a proof project (app with tests and deploy, RAG with benchmark, bounded agent with traces).
Decode 10 to 15 JDs into requirement, frequency, evidence, gap, next action; tier each Core, Role-specific or Stretch and choose study and mock topics from the tally.
Count frequency by job description, not by mentions, and read the sentences behind the keywords before trusting a tally.
Adapt only the top third of your resume, and never claim production experience or metrics you do not have.
Position as a software engineer who builds reliable AI products end to end, not as a beginner who has called an LLM API.
Baseline with three timed closed-book mocks (Python, SQL, DSA) and score process as well as result; justify every score of 3 or higher with an artifact.

check.q: You collected 12 job descriptions. Which approach best decides what to study first?
options: Study the newest framework mentioned in any posting
Tally requirements by how many JDs mention them, tier them, and start with Core rows where you have the biggest gap
Study only the topics you already enjoy
Copy the requirements list of the most senior posting
check.why: Frequency across JDs shows what the market consistently wants. Core requirements with the largest gaps give the best return; new frameworks change quickly and are replaceable once you know the concepts.

check.q: A recruiter asks what you built with LLMs, but your RAG project has only run on a public dataset. What is the best way to describe it?
options: Say it runs in production to sound stronger
Say 'we' throughout so ownership is unclear
Avoid details so no one can challenge them
State it as built and evaluated on a public dataset, say what you owned, and share what you measured
check.why: A true, precise account survives a deep dive. Inflated production claims are found quickly by follow-up questions and damage trust; honest scope plus measured results is persuasive.

check.q: Why is the 'Agentic AI Engineer' proof project described as a bounded agent with tests, traces and safe execution?
options: Interviewers look for evidence of control: limits, observability and security, not just a demo that works once
Agents cannot be tested, so traces replace tests
Bounded agents are the only kind frameworks support
Unbounded agents are cheaper to run
check.why: Agent roles are about reliability and safety: step limits, approvals, tracing and sandboxed side effects. A bounded, tested, traceable agent shows engineering control rather than a one-off demo.

parts.body:
> **Outcome:** Choose 3 role families; collect 10 job descriptions; baseline Python, SQL and DSA mock; record current gaps.
> **Prerequisites:** None. Start here.
> **Estimated time:** 40 min reading, then the hands-on task. Produce: Role matrix + gap tracker.

## Why start with a baseline and a position

Most candidates start by studying everything: every framework, every paper, every new model. That burns months and produces a flat, shallow profile. The better first move, this week, is to decide **what you are applying for** and **where you stand against it today**. Everything after this (the Python, SQL, RAG and agent weeks) is then aimed rather than random.

Two outputs this week: a **role matrix** (which role families, backed by real job descriptions) and a **gap tracker** (requirement by requirement: how often it appears, what evidence you have, what is missing, what you will do about it).

## The five role families

Titles are inconsistent across companies, so think in families by what the job actually does. Pick at most three: one primary, one adjacent, one stretch.

| Family | What the work is | What interviews stress | Proof project that persuades |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Software Engineer, AI** | Software engineering with AI integrated: APIs, data, testing, cloud, a feature that calls a model | Python/backend, SQL, system design, testing, reliability | A production-style AI app with auth, tests, logs and a deployment |
| **GenAI / LLM Engineer** | RAG, embeddings, retrieval, evaluation, model APIs, latency and cost | LLM fundamentals, retrieval design, evals, trade-offs | A RAG project with a benchmark and a written failure analysis |
| **AI Application Engineer** | End-to-end AI workflows as products: product reasoning plus reliable backends | System design, product trade-offs, backend reliability, metrics | A working app with metrics and documented trade-offs |
| **Agentic AI Engineer** | Tool use, state, orchestration, approvals, tracing, security | Agent design, failure handling, safety, prompt injection | A bounded agent with tests, traces and safe execution |
| **AI Platform / LLMOps (stretch)** | Deployment, monitoring, queues, cost controls, model serving | Infrastructure, observability, scaling, cost | A containerised service with a runbook |

How to choose: take the family where your existing experience already carries the most weight (for a backend engineer, usually the first or third), add the adjacent one that shares most skills, and keep one stretch family you will build toward. A backend engineer with four years should rarely target research or pure data-science roles; the leverage is engineering depth plus applied AI.

## Decoding job descriptions: the method

A job description is a list of guesses by the employer. Read enough of them and the pattern shows what the market actually wants.

1. **Collect 10 to 15 JDs** across your target families and companies you would genuinely accept. Save the text (links die).
2. **Open a spreadsheet** with columns: *requirement*, *frequency* (in how many JDs), *your evidence*, *gap*, *next action*.
3. **Extract requirements** as short nouns (Python, Postgres, RAG, evaluation, tracing). Merge synonyms. Ignore boilerplate such as "strong communication".
4. **Count frequency** by JD, not by mention.
5. **Tier each row:** **Core** (appears in most JDs of your primary family), **Role-specific** (appears in one family only), **Stretch** (rare or "nice to have").
6. **Fill evidence honestly:** a project, a mock result, a repo, a number you measured. Blank is a valid answer; it becomes the gap.
7. **Pick the next action** for each gap that is Core first: a lesson, a build, a mock.
8. **Choose mock and study topics from the tally**, not from the latest framework announcements. If 9 of 12 JDs say evaluation and 1 says a specific orchestration library, study evaluation.

Rules that keep you credible:
- Adapt the **top third of your resume** (headline, summary, first bullets) to the family; do not rewrite the whole thing for every posting.
- **Never claim production experience you lack.** "Built and load-tested a RAG service on a public dataset" is strong and true; "ran LLMs in production" when you did not is a trap that the project deep dive will find within five minutes.
- Do not chase every framework. Interviewers test concepts (retrieval, evaluation, state, failure handling), and any framework is replaceable.

## Positioning: the sentence you are building toward

Do not present as a beginner who has only called an LLM API. Present as **a software engineer who can build reliable AI products end to end**: you design the interface, the data model, the retrieval, the evaluation, the failure handling and the deployment, and you can say what you measured.

A structure that works: *who you are* (backend engineer, N years), *what you build* (AI features with retrieval, evaluation and reliability), *proof* (one project with a number and a trade-off), *direction* (the family you want and why).

Illustrative example, to adapt (not to copy): "I'm a backend engineer with five years in Python and Postgres. Over the last months I've been building LLM-backed services end to end, most recently a document Q&A system with hybrid retrieval and a 40-question evaluation set, where I measured retrieval hit rate and found most failures were chunking, not the model. I'm looking for GenAI engineer roles where reliability and evaluation matter." Replace every detail with something true.

## The interview loop map

Loops differ by company, so use this as a planning map, not a promise. Durations are typical ranges.

| Stage | Typical length | What is tested | How you prepare |
|---|---|---|---|
| Recruiter screen | 20 to 30 min | story, motivation, logistics, salary range, basic fit | the transition story, three role-family answers |
| Coding / DSA | 45 to 60 min | arrays, hash maps, trees, graphs, complexity, clean code | daily DSA block |
| Python / backend / SQL | 45 to 60 min | idiomatic Python, APIs, async, testing, queries, indexes | weeks 2 to 4 of this plan |
| LLM / GenAI technical | 45 to 60 min | tokenization, attention, prompting versus RAG versus fine-tuning, evaluation | fundamentals weeks |
| Practical implementation | 60 to 90 min live, or a 2 to 4 hour take-home | build a small RAG, agent or API with tests | project builds |
| System design | 45 to 60 min | multi-tenant doc assistant, cost, latency, reliability, security | design drills |
| Project deep dive | 45 to 60 min | your own project: decisions, failures, numbers, what you would change | project stories |
| Behavioral | 30 to 45 min | conflict, ownership, failure, ambiguity | STAR stories |
| Hiring manager | 30 to 45 min | scope, motivation, level, team fit | positioning plus questions to ask |

## Baseline self-assessment: how to measure where you stand

Run three short closed-book mocks this week, each in a plain editor with a timer, and score the **process** as well as the result.

- **Python mock, 45 min:** 3 small tasks (text cleaning, dedupe, a retry decorator). Note whether you tested, handled edge cases, explained complexity.
- **SQL mock, 30 min:** latest-per-user, a join with aggregation, a window function. Note NULL and tie handling.
- **DSA mock, 45 min:** two medium problems (a hash-map and a sliding-window or tree problem). Note time, hints used, correctness.

Then rate every area from 0 to 5 using the same scale for all domains:

| Score | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | not studied |
| 1 | recognise terms |
| 2 | explain with notes |
| 3 | explain closed-book |
| 4 | implement and debug |
| 5 | handle follow-ups |

Areas to rate: Python, SQL, DSA, backend/API, LLM fundamentals, RAG, evaluation, agents, system design, project story, behavioural stories, resume. Be harsh: most people overrate by one point. A score is justified only by an artifact (mock result, code you wrote, an answer you gave aloud).

## Failure modes

Too many target families (three is the cap); collecting JDs but never tallying; scoring yourself from memory instead of from a mock; targeting trendy frameworks over concepts; writing a position statement with claims you cannot defend in a deep dive; treating the baseline as a one-time exercise instead of re-running it every few weeks.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Concepts tab: a failure born from misunderstanding the idea, a follow-up that probes the definition, and the extra theory you would drop. A candidate collected 40 job descriptions, highlighted every tool name, and wrote a position statement that claimed 'built production RAG' after a weekend notebook. In the first screen they could not name a metric, a failure, or which three role families they were actually targeting. The baseline mock (Python, SQL, a 45-minute array problem) scored 2/5 on framing because they started coding before restating the question. The tracker existed as a spreadsheet of links, not as a scored gap list. Two weeks later they were still 'researching titles' and had no artifact they could defend.

## Interview follow-up

Ask this after you close the tab. Interviewer: 'Walk me through how you chose this role family over applied scientist or platform.' Outline: name the three families you kept, the JD phrases that decided it (evals vs training vs serving), one family you cut and why, and the gap you will close first. If they ask 'have you shipped this?', answer with what you actually shipped, what was a prototype, and the next proof you will have by week four. Do not invent a title you cannot defend.

## What you would cut

If this part is running long, drop background that does not change a decision. Cut the fourth role family, the tool-name highlighter pass, and any claim that is not backed by a dated mock or a repo you can open. Keep ten decoded JDs, three families, one scored baseline, and a tracker with owners and dates.

parts.body:
## The proof artifact: role matrix plus gap tracker

You will produce two files: `role_matrix.yaml` (your three role families with evidence and gaps) and `gap_tracker.yaml` (one row per requirement). The three code blocks are a tally script and the two templates. A spreadsheet works equally well; the point is that the data is written down and re-run, not carried in your head.

## A worked JD analysis (illustrative, invented JDs)

The five mini job descriptions below are **invented for teaching**. They are shorter than real ones but phrased the way real ones are. Real JDs are longer and noisier, which makes the tally more important, not less.

1. *Software Engineer, AI.* Python, REST APIs, SQL, AWS. Integrate LLM APIs into product features. Unit tests, CI/CD. Docker.
2. *GenAI Engineer.* RAG pipelines: embeddings, vector database, retrieval. Evaluation and benchmarks. Python, LLMs, prompt design. Logging.
3. *AI Application Engineer.* Python, FastAPI, REST API design, Postgres. LLM workflows, prompt iteration, evaluation. Cloud deployment, monitoring. Testing.
4. *Agentic AI Engineer.* Tool use and function calling, orchestration (LangGraph), tracing and observability. Python, LLMs, evals, Docker.
5. *AI Platform Engineer.* Kubernetes, Docker, AWS, LLMOps, model serving (vLLM), monitoring, CI/CD. Python. Some RAG exposure.

Running `python jd_tally.py` on these gives:

| Requirement | JDs of 5 | Tier (at least 60 percent is Core, 30 to 59 percent Role-specific, below that Stretch) |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 5 | Core |
| LLM APIs | 4 | Core |
| Monitoring / observability | 4 | Core |
| Cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure) | 3 | Core |
| Docker / containers | 3 | Core |
| Evaluation | 3 | Core |
| Testing / CI | 3 | Core |
| RAG / retrieval | 2 | Role-specific |
| REST / API design | 2 | Role-specific |
| SQL / Postgres | 2 | Role-specific |
| Agents / tool use | 1 | Stretch |
| MLOps / serving | 1 | Stretch |

### What this teaches you to do

- **The tally is only as good as the sample.** Five JDs spanning five families is a demonstration; your real sample should be 10 to 15 JDs, weighted towards your primary family. Tiers are relative to your sample, so re-tier after you pick a family: inside the GenAI family, retrieval and evaluation would be Core.
- **Keyword counting is a first pass.** A regex says "Monitoring" appears; you still read the sentence to see whether it means dashboards or tracing LLM calls. Use the script to find the shape, then read the top requirements by hand.
- **Rows that appear everywhere beat rows that look impressive.** Python, LLM integration, monitoring and testing show up in nearly every JD here; fancy topics such as serving appear once.

### Turning rows into a gap tracker

Take three rows and write them the way the tracker expects. Suppose your honest facts are: a solid backend, one small RAG demo, no evaluation set, no experience with serving.

| Requirement | Frequency | Your evidence | Gap | Next action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluation | 3 of 5 | none yet | no benchmark, no failure analysis | build a 30-question eval set for the RAG project, report hit rate |
| Monitoring / observability | 4 of 5 | request logging in a past backend service | no tracing of LLM calls, no cost metrics | add structured logs with token counts and latency to the project |
| MLOps / serving | 1 of 5 | none | all of it | Stretch: defer; revisit when you reach the LLMOps week |

Note what the process did: evaluation, not serving, got this week's attention, and the "next action" is a concrete build, not "learn more".

## Using the templates

`role_matrix.yaml` records, per family, the typical titles, core skills, the proof project and the evidence you really have. `gap_tracker.yaml` has the columns from the method plus a 0 to 5 score and a due date. Update both every Sunday during the weekly review. Two rules: a score of 3 or higher needs a mock result or an answer you gave closed-book; a gap is deleted only when its evidence exists.

## The baseline mock log

Alongside the files, keep a short log of the three baseline mocks. Record date, duration, tasks, what you finished, what you needed hints for, and two process notes (for example "did not write tests", "forgot empty input", "could not explain complexity"). In five weeks you will repeat the same mocks with new problems and compare; the improvement in process notes is the most reliable signal you have.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Worked example tab: a failure in the numbers or the code, a follow-up that changes a constraint, and the step you would skip under time. A candidate collected 40 job descriptions, highlighted every tool name, and wrote a position statement that claimed 'built production RAG' after a weekend notebook. In the first screen they could not name a metric, a failure, or which three role families they were actually targeting. The baseline mock (Python, SQL, a 45-minute array problem) scored 2/5 on framing because they started coding before restating the question. The tracker existed as a spreadsheet of links, not as a scored gap list. Two weeks later they were still 'researching titles' and had no artifact they could defend.

## Interview follow-up

The interviewer just changed one number in the example. Interviewer: 'Walk me through how you chose this role family over applied scientist or platform.' Outline: name the three families you kept, the JD phrases that decided it (evals vs training vs serving), one family you cut and why, and the gap you will close first. If they ask 'have you shipped this?', answer with what you actually shipped, what was a prototype, and the next proof you will have by week four. Do not invent a title you cannot defend.

## What you would cut

Ship the smallest version of this example that still teaches the mechanism. Cut the fourth role family, the tool-name highlighter pass, and any claim that is not backed by a dated mock or a repo you can open. Keep ten decoded JDs, three families, one scored baseline, and a tracker with owners and dates.

# jd_tally.py -- count how often each requirement appears across job descriptions.
# Usage: put one JD per file in jds/*.txt and run `python jd_tally.py jds`; with no argument it
# runs on the five short ILLUSTRATIVE (invented) JDs below.
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

REQUIREMENTS: dict[str, str] = {   # requirement -> regex of the ways JDs phrase it
    "Python": r"\bpython\b",
    "REST / API design": r"\b(rest|restful|api design|apis?)\b",
    "SQL / Postgres": r"\b(sql|postgres(?:ql)?)\b",
    "Cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure)": r"\b(aws|gcp|azure|cloud)\b",
    "Docker / containers": r"\b(docker|container(?:s|ized)?|kubernetes)\b",
    "Testing / CI": r"\b(unit tests?|testing|ci/cd|pytest)\b",
    "LLM APIs": r"\b(llms?|openai|anthropic|model apis?|prompt\w*)\b",
    "RAG / retrieval": r"\b(rag|retrieval|vector (?:search|database|db)|embeddings?)\b",
    "Evaluation": r"\b(evals?|evaluation|benchmark\w*)\b",
    "Agents / tool use": r"\b(agents?|agentic|tool use|function calling|orchestration|langgraph)\b",
    "Monitoring / observability": r"\b(monitoring|observability|tracing|logging)\b",
    "MLOps / serving": r"\b(mlops|llmops|model serving|vllm|inference)\b",
}

SAMPLE_JDS = [
    "Software Engineer, AI. Python, REST APIs, SQL, AWS. Integrate LLM APIs into product features. Write unit tests, CI/CD. Docker.",
    "GenAI Engineer. Build RAG pipelines: embeddings, vector database, retrieval. Evaluation and benchmarks. Python, LLMs, prompt design. Logging.",
    "AI Application Engineer. Python, FastAPI, REST API design, Postgres. LLM workflows, prompt iteration, evaluation. Cloud deployment, monitoring. Testing.",
    "Agentic AI Engineer. Tool use and function calling, orchestration (LangGraph), tracing and observability. Python, LLMs, evals, Docker.",
    "AI Platform Engineer. Kubernetes, Docker, AWS, LLMOps, model serving (vLLM), monitoring, CI/CD. Python. Some RAG exposure.",
]


def load_jds(folder: str | None) -> list[str]:
    if folder is None:
        return SAMPLE_JDS
    texts = [p.read_text(encoding="utf-8") for p in sorted(Path(folder).glob("*.txt"))]
    if not texts:
        raise SystemExit(f"no .txt files in {folder}")
    return texts


def tally(jds: list[str]) -> list[tuple[str, int, str]]:
    rows = []
    for name, pattern in REQUIREMENTS.items():
        rx = re.compile(pattern, re.IGNORECASE)
        hits = sum(1 for jd in jds if rx.search(jd))   # count JDs, not mentions
        share = hits / len(jds)
        tier = "Core" if share >= 0.6 else "Role-specific" if share >= 0.3 else "Stretch"
        rows.append((name, hits, tier))
    return sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (-r[1], r[0]))


def main() -> None:
    jds = load_jds(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else None)
    print(f"{len(jds)} job descriptions")
    print(f"{'requirement':28} {'JDs':>4}  tier")
    for name, hits, tier in tally(jds):
        print(f"{name:28} {hits:>4}  {tier}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# role_matrix.yaml -- your positioning decision. Fill it in after you tally 10-15 real JDs.
# Rule: at most three role families; one primary, one adjacent, one stretch.
generated: 2026-10-26            # re-do every 4-6 weeks
jds_collected: 12                # how many real JDs you read (replace with your number)

families:
  - name: Software Engineer, AI
    priority: primary
    jd_count: 0                  # how many of your JDs fit this family
    typical_titles: ["Software Engineer, AI", "Backend Engineer, AI Platform"]
    core_skills: [python, apis, sql, testing, cloud, llm-integration]
    proof_project: "Production-style AI app: auth, tests, logs, deploy"
    have_evidence: []            # real things you can show, one line each
    gaps: []
  - name: GenAI / LLM Engineer
    priority: adjacent
    jd_count: 0
    typical_titles: ["GenAI Engineer", "LLM Engineer", "Applied AI Engineer"]
    core_skills: [rag, embeddings, retrieval, evaluation, model-apis, latency-cost]
    proof_project: "RAG project with benchmark and failure analysis"
    have_evidence: []
    gaps: []
  - name: Agentic AI Engineer
    priority: stretch
    jd_count: 0
    typical_titles: ["Agentic AI Engineer", "AI Agent Engineer"]
    core_skills: [tool-use, state, orchestration, approvals, tracing, security]
    proof_project: "Bounded agent with tests, traces and safe execution"
    have_evidence: []
    gaps: []

resume_top_third:                # headline + summary + first two bullets, rewritten per family
  headline: "Software engineer building reliable AI products end to end"
  never_claim: ["production LLM traffic you did not run", "metrics you did not measure"]

# gap_tracker.yaml -- one row per requirement. Update weekly, delete rows only when proven.
# tier: core | role-specific | stretch      score: 0-5 (0 not studied ... 5 handles follow-ups)
- requirement: Python coding (strings, dict/set, typing)
  tier: core
  frequency: "10/12 JDs"
  evidence: "Baseline mock 2026-10-26: solved 2 of 3 in 40 min"
  score: 3
  gap: "Slow on edge cases; no tests written during the mock"
  next_action: "10 exercises with tests, week of Nov 2"
  due: 2026-11-08
- requirement: SQL (windows, indexes, transactions)
  tier: core
  frequency: "8/12 JDs"
  evidence: "Mock: latest-per-user solved with hints"
  score: 2
  gap: "Cannot read EXPLAIN output; isolation levels fuzzy"
  next_action: "Timed 8-problem set plus one explained plan, week of Nov 16"
  due: 2026-11-22
- requirement: RAG evaluation
  tier: role-specific
  frequency: "6/12 JDs"
  evidence: "None yet"
  score: 1
  gap: "No benchmark or failure analysis to show"
  next_action: "Build the RAG project with a 30-question eval set"
  due: 2026-12-20

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
These are story questions, so the model answers below are **templates with blanks in square brackets**. Fill every blank with something true. Never invent a metric, employer, scale or production claim; an interviewer who probes a made-up detail ends the interview there. If you lack a piece of experience, say so and describe how you validated or would validate it.

## Q1. Walk me through your transition into AI engineering

- **Define:** A 90-second story that explains where you came from, what you built to cross over, and where you are heading, so the interviewer sees a deliberate path rather than a trend chase.
- **Mechanism:** Four beats: *foundation* (your engineering background and one thing you are good at), *trigger* (what drew you to AI work, concretely), *proof* (what you built or learned, with one real result), *direction* (the role family and what you want to own).
- **Decision:** Lead with engineering strength, because it is the scarce skill. Mention study only as the means to a built thing. Pick one proof project rather than listing five.
- **Trade-off:** A long chronological story loses people; a very short one sounds rehearsed. Aim for 90 seconds and invite a deeper question.
- **Evidence:** One project you can discuss for 20 minutes, with a decision you changed because of a measurement.

**Failure mode to mention:** apologising ("I'm just a backend dev") or inflating ("I've been doing AI for years"). Both break trust.

**60-90 second version (template):** "I'm a [backend / full-stack] engineer with [N] years in [Python, Postgres, whatever is true]; the thing I'm best at is [reliability / data modelling / APIs]. I got interested in LLM systems when [a concrete trigger, such as a feature at work or a personal project]. Since then I've built [project], which [does X] using [retrieval / tool calling], and I measured [a real metric, or: I built an evaluation set of N questions and found Y]. What I learned is that [one real lesson, for example most failures came from retrieval, not the model]. I'm now looking for [role family] roles where [reliability and evaluation matter], because that's where my engineering background adds the most."

**Follow-ups:**
- *What have you shipped, versus experimented with?* Answer precisely. "Shipped" means real users; "built and tested on a public dataset" is a perfectly good honest alternative.
- *What was the hardest part?* Pick a technical decision with a trade-off, not a tool problem.
- *What do you still not know?* Name one real gap and the plan you are following to close it (this is your gap tracker).

## Q2. Why this role family and not a data-science role?

- **Define:** Explain that you chose a role where the output is a working, reliable software system built on models, rather than analysis or model training.
- **Mechanism:** Contrast the daily work. Data science centres on analysis, experiments, statistical modelling and sometimes training models; applied AI engineering centres on integrating existing models into products: retrieval, tool use, evaluation, latency, cost, reliability, deployment.
- **Decision:** Tie it to evidence: your strengths (systems, APIs, data pipelines), what you enjoy (building and operating things), and what the family needs (the JD requirements you tallied).
- **Trade-off:** You give up deep model-training work and some research exposure; you gain ownership of end-to-end behaviour. Acknowledge that the boundary is blurry and that you understand the statistics you need for evaluation.
- **Evidence:** Your JD tally: "Of the [N] postings I studied, [k] emphasised [Python services, evaluation, deployment] rather than [model training or statistical modelling]."

**Failure mode to mention:** disparaging data science, or implying you avoid maths. Say instead that evaluation, sampling and metric design are part of the job.

**60-90 second version (template):** "I read [N] job descriptions for AI roles and sorted them by what the work is. The role I'm targeting is mostly about building systems around existing models: retrieval, tool calling, evaluation, latency and cost, and operating them reliably. That's where my [N] years of backend work matter. A data-science role is more about analysis and modelling, which is valuable but not what I want to spend my days on. I still do the statistical work that applied AI needs: for [project] I built an evaluation set and tracked [hit rate / answer quality] across changes. If a role needs heavy model training, I'd be honest that I'm not the strongest fit today."

**Follow-ups:**
- *Do you know the maths behind attention and embeddings?* Give the working-level explanation and say you can go deeper on request.
- *Would you fine-tune a model?* Yes when prompting and retrieval are not enough and you have data and an evaluation to prove it helps; say how you would decide.
- *Isn't an LLM engineer just calling an API?* Describe what sits around the call: retrieval, validation, evals, retries, cost control, observability.

## Q3. What have you built with LLMs and what exactly was your part?

- **Define:** A precise, ownership-clear account of one project: the problem, your design, your code, the result, and what you would change.
- **Mechanism:** Use five parts: *problem and user*, *architecture in one sentence* (components and data flow), *your part* ("I wrote X and Y; a teammate did Z"), *evidence* (a measurement or a failure you analysed), *what you would change*.
- **Decision:** Choose the project with the most defensible decisions, not the flashiest. Prepare numbers you actually measured and label them (for example "on my 40-question set").
- **Trade-off:** More detail proves depth but needs preparation; vague answers sound inflated. Be ready for the deep dive: every component you mention may be probed.
- **Evidence:** A repository, a short architecture diagram, an evaluation table, and one honest failure analysis.

**Failure mode to mention:** saying "we" for everything, so the interviewer cannot tell what you did, or claiming production usage for a demo.

**60-90 second version (template):** "The project I know best is [name], a [what it does] for [who]. The flow is [ingest, chunk, embed, retrieve, generate with citations], backed by [Postgres + pgvector / other]. My part was [the retrieval layer and the evaluation harness / the API and tests / everything, since it was a solo project]. I measured it on [N questions I wrote]: [hit rate / faithfulness result, only if real]. The biggest finding was [a real failure, such as chunk size splitting a table]. If I did it again I'd [specific change]. It's [a personal project / a prototype / in production for N users, whichever is true]."

**Follow-ups:**
- *How did you evaluate it?* Describe the dataset, the metric, and how you avoided tuning to the test set.
- *What broke?* Have one concrete failure and its fix.
- *How would you scale it to 100x the documents?* Talk through indexing, filtering, latency and cost at a high level, flagged as what you would validate.

## Q4 (added). What is your biggest gap right now, and what are you doing about it?

- **Define:** A calm, specific statement of a real gap with a dated plan.
- **Mechanism:** Gap, impact, plan, evidence of progress. Pull directly from your gap tracker.
- **Decision:** Choose a gap that is real but not disqualifying for the role (for example "I haven't run LLM serving infrastructure; I know the concepts and I'm building a small containerised service this month").
- **Trade-off:** Too trivial a gap sounds evasive; a core-skill gap sounds alarming. Pick a Role-specific or Stretch item.
- **Evidence:** The tracker row and one thing you already completed towards it.

**Failure mode to mention:** "I'm a perfectionist" style non-answers.

**60-90 second version (template):** "The one I'm closing now is [gap]. It matters because [how it affects the work]. I'm handling it by [specific build or study with a date], and so far I've [done X]. For the interview loop, it means I can discuss [the concepts] and would validate [the practical bit] on the job."

**Follow-ups:** *How do you prioritise learning?* From job-description frequency and from mock-interview scores. *What would a good first 90 days look like?* Understand the system, ship a small improvement, add an evaluation.

## Q5 (added). Why would you be a better hire than someone with a research or ML background?

- **Define:** Position your edge as production engineering applied to AI, without putting the other candidate down.
- **Mechanism:** Reliability, testing, data modelling, API design, debugging distributed behaviour, cost and latency awareness: these decide whether an AI feature survives contact with users.
- **Decision:** Say what you would pair with a research colleague: they bring modelling depth, you bring the system around it.
- **Trade-off:** You may need to learn some modelling depth; state how you are doing that.
- **Evidence:** A project where reliability work (retries, validation, evals, logging) changed an outcome.

**Failure mode to mention:** claiming that engineering matters more than research. Say that both matter and teams need the combination.

**60-90 second version (template):** "Models are one component. The rest is the system: validation, retries, evaluation, monitoring, permissions and cost. That's my background. For example, in [project] [a true reliability improvement]. I'd happily work with someone with deeper modelling expertise; I'd make sure what we build is testable, observable and shippable."

**Follow-ups:** *What's your plan to deepen the ML side?* Name the fundamentals weeks and one concrete resource. *Which would you rather own, evals or infra?* Answer honestly with a reason.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Interview tab: a spoken-answer failure, the actual next question, and the essay you would not say out loud. A candidate collected 40 job descriptions, highlighted every tool name, and wrote a position statement that claimed 'built production RAG' after a weekend notebook. In the first screen they could not name a metric, a failure, or which three role families they were actually targeting. The baseline mock (Python, SQL, a 45-minute array problem) scored 2/5 on framing because they started coding before restating the question. The tracker existed as a spreadsheet of links, not as a scored gap list. Two weeks later they were still 'researching titles' and had no artifact they could defend.

## Interview follow-up

You already gave a 90-second answer; this is the probe. Interviewer: 'Walk me through how you chose this role family over applied scientist or platform.' Outline: name the three families you kept, the JD phrases that decided it (evals vs training vs serving), one family you cut and why, and the gap you will close first. If they ask 'have you shipped this?', answer with what you actually shipped, what was a prototype, and the next proof you will have by week four. Do not invent a title you cannot defend.

## What you would cut

Say less: keep define, mechanism, decision, trade-off, evidence. Cut the fourth role family, the tool-name highlighter pass, and any claim that is not backed by a dated mock or a repo you can open. Keep ten decoded JDs, three families, one scored baseline, and a tracker with owners and dates.

lessons.summary: Write correct, tested Python without autocomplete: data structures and complexity, text and chunking helpers, retries, caches, generators, typing and exceptions.
keyPoints: Set and dict operations are O(1) on average; list membership is O(n), so move repeated lookups into a set.
Default argument values are evaluated once, so use None and build the mutable object inside the function.
Dict keys and set members must be hashable: stable hash plus consistent equality, which excludes list, dict and set.
Generators are lazy and single pass; use them for streams and batches, lists when you need len, indexing or reuse.
Treat model output as untrusted: extract, parse, validate types, and raise one domain exception the caller can handle.
Chunking with overlap steps by size minus overlap; validate parameters and avoid emitting a duplicate tail window.
Retry only retryable exceptions, with exponential backoff, jitter and an injectable sleep so tests run instantly.
Name edge cases aloud and write asserts before running: empty input, k of 0, duplicates, zero vectors.

check.q: You call `if doc_id in seen_ids` for each of 100,000 documents, where `seen_ids` is a list of 100,000 ids. What is the best fix?
options: Sort the list once and keep calling `in`
Use a generator expression for `seen_ids`
Store the ids in a set, giving O(1) average membership
Convert `seen_ids` to a tuple
check.why: List membership scans every element (O(n) per check, O(n squared) overall). A set hashes the id, so each check is O(1) on average. A tuple is also a linear scan and sorting does not change what `in` does.

check.q: What does this print? `def f(x, acc=[]): acc.append(x); return acc` then `f(1); print(f(2))`
options: An error because the default is mutable
check.why: The default list is created once at definition time and shared by all calls that omit `acc`, so the second call sees the 1 already appended. Python does not raise an error; the fix is a None default.

check.q: A retry decorator wraps a model call and catches `Exception`. Which problem does this create?
options: It cannot retry network timeouts
It retries programmer errors such as KeyError, wasting time and hiding bugs
It makes the function a generator
It prevents the last attempt from raising
check.why: Catching every Exception retries permanent errors too (bad input, bugs). Retry only specific retryable types such as timeouts or 429/5xx wrappers, and re-raise the original error on the final attempt.

parts.label: Concepts
parts.body:
> **Outcome:** Strings, dict/set, functions, exceptions, typing; solve small coding tasks without IDE autocomplete.
> **Prerequisites:** Baseline week done; basic Python syntax.
> **Estimated time:** 45 min reading, then the hands-on task. Produce: 10 Python exercises + review notes.

## What the Python round actually tests

The Python screen for an AI-engineering role is rarely a hard algorithm puzzle. It is a 30 to 45 minute check that you can write correct, readable Python quickly and without an IDE holding your hand. Typical prompts are small: clean and tokenise text, count words, deduplicate records, group rows, split a document into overlapping chunks, parse a model's JSON reply, add a retry, build a small cache. Interviewers watch four things: do you clarify the input, do you pick the right data structure, do you handle edge cases without being prompted, and can you test what you wrote.

This week you build the muscle for that: 10 exercises, written closed-book, each with tests, plus review notes on every mistake.

## The core data structures (know the complexity cold)

| Type | Mutable | Ordered | Hashable | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `list` | yes | yes (insertion) | no | sequence you append to, index into, sort |
| `tuple` | no | yes | yes, if all items are hashable | fixed record, dict key, return several values |
| `set` | yes | no guarantee | no (`frozenset` is) | membership tests, dedupe, set algebra |
| `dict` | yes | yes (insertion order, guaranteed since 3.7) | no | lookup by key, counting, grouping |

Complexity of common operations (CPython; "average" for hash tables, because a pathological collision pattern degrades to O(n) but you will not meet it with normal keys):

| Operation | list | tuple | set | dict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| index `x[i]` | O(1) | O(1) | n/a | O(1) by key |
| `x in c` | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) avg | O(1) avg (keys) |
| append / add / set item | O(1) amortised | immutable | O(1) avg | O(1) avg |
| insert or delete at front | O(n) | immutable | n/a (unordered) | n/a (keyed) |
| `pop()` from end | O(1) | immutable | n/a | O(1) |
| `pop(0)` | O(n) | immutable | n/a | n/a |
| iterate | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) |
| sort | O(n log n) | `sorted()` gives a list | `sorted()` gives a list | `sorted()` of keys |

Two consequences you should say out loud in interviews. First, `if x in some_list` inside a loop turns an O(n) job into O(n squared); convert the list to a set once. Second, `list.pop(0)` and `list.insert(0, x)` shift every element, so use `collections.deque` for queues.

**Hashability.** A dict key or set member must have a hash that does not change while it is stored, and must compare equal to equal objects. Immutable built-ins (str, int, tuple of hashables, frozenset) qualify. `list`, `dict` and `set` do not, which is why `{[1, 2]: "x"}` raises `TypeError: unhashable type`. A tuple containing a list is also unhashable. A frozen dataclass is hashable; a normal dataclass with `eq=True` and `frozen=False` sets `__hash__` to `None`.

## Strings, text and the standard library you should reach for

Strings are immutable, so building one with `s += piece` in a loop can be quadratic in the worst case. Collect pieces in a list and `"".join(parts)`. Know `split()` (no argument splits on any whitespace run), `str.strip`, `str.casefold` (better than `lower` for comparison across languages), f-strings, and `re` basics: `re.findall`, `re.sub`, compiled patterns, groups.

From the standard library, these five cover most screens: `collections.Counter` and `defaultdict`, `heapq.nsmallest` / `nlargest` for top-k, `itertools` (`islice`, `chain`, `groupby`, which needs sorted input), `functools` (`lru_cache`, `wraps`, `partial`), and `dataclasses`. If an interviewer bans `Counter`, you should still be able to count with a plain dict in four lines.

A word on tokens: in LLM work a "token" is a sub-word unit produced by the model's tokenizer, not a whitespace word. Splitting on whitespace is fine for a coding exercise (the chunker takes a list of tokens either way), but say so: in production you would count with the model's tokenizer because context limits and cost are measured in model tokens.

## Functions, defaults and the mutable-default trap

Default argument values are evaluated once, when `def` runs, not on each call:

```python
def add_tag(tag, tags=[]):   # bug: one shared list for every call
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags

add_tag("a")  # ['a']
add_tag("b")  # ['a', 'b']  <- surprise
```

The fix is the `None` sentinel: `def add_tag(tag, tags=None): tags = [] if tags is None else tags`. The same bug appears as `def f(cache={})`, which is occasionally a deliberate memo, but then say so with a comment. Related traps: late binding in closures (`[lambda: i for i in range(3)]` all return 2; bind with `lambda i=i: i`), and mutating a list while iterating over it.

Also know `*args`, `**kwargs`, keyword-only arguments (`def f(a, *, b)`), and that functions are objects, which is what makes decorators work: a decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a function. Always use `functools.wraps` so the wrapped function keeps its name and docstring.

## Generators versus lists

A list holds all its items in memory. A generator (a function with `yield`, or a generator expression `(x for x in xs)`) produces items one at a time and can be consumed once. Use a generator when the data is large or streamed (reading a file line by line, batching documents for an embedding API, streaming model tokens), or when the consumer may stop early. Use a list when you need `len`, indexing, repeated passes or sorting.

Worked number: tokenising 1,000,000 short documents into lists of tokens might hold hundreds of megabytes (every token is a separate Python object, roughly 50+ bytes each; treat that as an order-of-magnitude estimate). A generator pipeline holds one document at a time.

When it breaks: a generator is exhausted after one pass, so `g = (x for x in xs); len(list(g)); list(g)` gives an empty second list. Errors inside a generator surface when it is consumed, not when it is created, so argument validation placed in the generator body runs late. Validate eagerly in a normal function that returns the generator if you need early failure.

## Exceptions: how to design them

- Catch the narrowest exception you can handle. A bare `except:` also catches `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`; `except Exception:` that swallows everything hides bugs.
- Define your own small hierarchy for your domain, for example `class ModelOutputError(ValueError)`. Callers then catch what they understand and let the rest propagate.
- Chain causes with `raise NewError("context") from original` so the traceback keeps both.
- Use `finally` or a context manager (`with`) for cleanup. Do not use exceptions for ordinary control flow in hot loops, and do not return `None` to signal failure when the caller will forget to check.
- Separate retryable failures (timeout, 429, 5xx) from permanent ones (400, validation). A retry decorator that catches `Exception` will happily retry a `KeyError` three times.

## Type hints

Type hints are not enforced at runtime, but they document intent and let `mypy` or `pyright` catch bugs. In an interview, annotate function signatures: `def top_k(query: Sequence[float], k: int) -> list[Hit]`. Use built-in generics (`list[str]`, `dict[str, int]`, `X | None`) on Python 3.10+. Use `TypeVar` for functions that return the same type they take, `Callable[[A], B]` for function arguments, `Iterator[T]` for generators, and `Sequence` for "anything indexable" arguments so callers can pass lists or tuples.

## `dataclass` versus `dict`

A `dict` is flexible and cheap, but its shape is invisible: a typo in a key is a runtime `KeyError` far from the cause. A `dataclass` gives named, typed fields, a generated `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__`, and `frozen=True` makes instances immutable and hashable. Use dicts at the edges (JSON in, JSON out) and convert to dataclasses (or pydantic models, which also validate) once inside your code. Dataclasses do not validate types at runtime; pydantic does.

## Decision guide

| Situation | Choose |
|---|---|
| Fast membership test, dedupe | `set` (or `dict` keys to keep order) |
| Need order and duplicates | `list` |
| Fixed record or dict key | `tuple` / frozen dataclass |
| Count or group | `dict` / `Counter` / `defaultdict` |
| Big or streaming data | generator |
| Queue with pops from the front | `collections.deque` |
| Internal structured data | dataclass; validated external input: pydantic |

## Failure modes to check before you say "done"

Empty input, one element, duplicates, `k` larger than the data, `k = 0`, negative numbers, `None` where a string is expected, unicode and punctuation, and invalid parameters (overlap not smaller than size). Say them aloud before the interviewer asks; it is the single biggest signal that you write production code.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Concepts tab: a failure born from misunderstanding the idea, a follow-up that probes the definition, and the extra theory you would drop. In a 35-minute screen the candidate wrote a correct-looking group-by on a list of events, then froze when asked the complexity of `list.pop(0)` and why a `set` membership test was in the inner loop. They had practised only with autocomplete. The function mutated a default-argument dict, so a second call leaked keys from the first. They could not write a 4-line test for the empty input. The review notes said 'need more LeetCode' instead of naming the three language gaps: mutation, iterators, and exceptions.

## Interview follow-up

Ask this after you close the tab. Interviewer: 'This function is called on a 10 GB log. What breaks, and what do you change?' Outline: name the materializing comprehension, switch to a generator or line iterator, say why `dict` not list for the lookup, and mention a test for a truncated last line. Follow-up: 'What does your type hint guarantee?' Answer: it documents intent; runtime still needs a check or a pydantic model if this is an API.

## What you would cut

If this part is running long, drop background that does not change a decision. Cut IDE autocomplete for the ten exercises, the sixth rewrite of the same two-sum, and any solution you cannot explain without the tab. Keep one timed set, the error log (pattern, edge, complexity, bug), and a re-solve date.

parts.body:
## The proof artifact: 10 exercises plus review notes

The artifact for this week is a folder with ten solved exercises, a test for each, and a one-page `review.md`. The four code blocks below are a reference solution set. Do not copy them first. Run the protocol:

1. Pick an exercise by its docstring only. Use a plain editor with no autocomplete, or paper.
2. Set a timer. Give yourself 8 minutes for the easy ones (1 to 4), 12 for the rest.
3. Say the edge cases aloud, write the function, then write 3 to 6 asserts before running anything.
4. Run it. Every failure goes into `review.md` as one line: what broke, why, the rule that would have prevented it.
5. Only then compare with the reference and note differences in approach, not just in syntax.

Save the four blocks as `exercises_a.py` to `exercises_d.py` and the last block as `run_all.py`. `python run_all.py` runs all ten test groups with the standard library only (Python 3.10 or newer, because of `X | None` and `ParamSpec`).

Edge cases to name per exercise: empty input and punctuation-only text (1); k of 0 and k above the unique count (2); dicts as items for `dedupe` (3); empty input for `group_by` (4); overlap not below size and input shorter than a window (5); fences, prose around JSON, missing field, `True` passing as `int` (6); retrying the wrong exception (7); get refreshing recency (8); partial last batch (9); zero vector and dimension mismatch (10).

## Walkthrough of the non-obvious choices

**Exercise 2: why a heap.** Sorting all `n` unique words costs O(n log n). `heapq.nsmallest(k, ...)` keeps a heap of size `k`, so it is about O(n log k). Negating the count lets `nsmallest` return the highest counts while the word breaks ties alphabetically, which makes the output deterministic (tests can compare exact lists). If asked for the follow-up "what if the text does not fit in memory", the answer is to stream tokens into the counting dict (memory scales with unique words, not total words), and beyond that use an approximate structure such as a count-min sketch. Name it, do not implement it.

**Exercise 5: the chunker.** With `size=4`, `overlap=1` the step is 3, so windows start at 0, 3, 6 and the 10-token input yields `abcd`, `defg`, `ghij`. Overlap exists so a fact that straddles a boundary appears whole in at least one chunk. The early `break` stops once a window reaches the end of the input; without it, `size=4, overlap=2` on 6 tokens would emit a third window that is entirely contained in the second. In RAG, chunk by model tokens and respect sentence or heading boundaries when you can; this exercise is the arithmetic core.

**Exercise 6: untrusted model output.** The model may wrap JSON in prose or markdown fences, may omit fields, or may produce `true` where you asked for a number. The function finds the outermost braces, parses, and validates names and types. Note `isinstance(True, int)` is `True` in Python, hence the explicit boolean check. It raises one domain exception, `ModelOutputError`, so the caller can decide to re-ask the model. In production you would use pydantic or the provider's structured-output feature and still keep this as the fallback path. Limitation worth stating: taking the text between the first `{` and the last `}` fails if the model emits two separate objects.

**Exercise 7: retry.** `sleep` is a parameter so the test records delays `[1.0, 2.0]` instead of waiting. The decorator retries only the exception types you list; the final attempt re-raises the original error. A real version adds jitter (a random fraction of the delay) so many clients do not retry in lockstep, honours a `Retry-After` header, and has a cap on total time. Those are the three follow-ups to be ready for.

**Exercise 8: LRU.** `OrderedDict` remembers insertion order and `move_to_end` / `popitem(last=False)` are O(1). Without it you build a dict plus a doubly linked list by hand (dict maps key to node, list orders by recency). `functools.lru_cache` does this for pure functions; a cache for LLM calls must key on the full request (model, prompt, parameters) and must not be shared across users for private inputs.

**Exercise 9: generators.** `batched` yields lists lazily: the shape you need to send documents to an embedding endpoint 64 at a time. Python 3.12 added `itertools.batched` (tuples); writing your own works everywhere.

**Exercise 10: similarity.** Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by the product of norms. A zero vector has no direction, so dividing would raise `ZeroDivisionError`; the function defines the result as 0.0 and the ranking is made deterministic by sorting on `(-score, doc_id)`. Brute force is O(n times d) per query. Say that approximate nearest-neighbour indexes (HNSW, IVF) trade a little recall for much lower latency once n is large, but that for a few thousand vectors brute force is fine and simpler.

## Writing your `review.md`

One row per mistake, including typos that cost you minutes: exercise, what went wrong, root cause, rule for next time (for example: "5, off-by-one in the last window, did not trace a small example, trace 10 tokens with size 4 and overlap 1 before coding"). Patterns appear after two or three rows (forgetting empty input, using `in` on a list, not testing the failing path). Those patterns are what you drill on Saturday.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Worked example tab: a failure in the numbers or the code, a follow-up that changes a constraint, and the step you would skip under time. In a 35-minute screen the candidate wrote a correct-looking group-by on a list of events, then froze when asked the complexity of `list.pop(0)` and why a `set` membership test was in the inner loop. They had practised only with autocomplete. The function mutated a default-argument dict, so a second call leaked keys from the first. They could not write a 4-line test for the empty input. The review notes said 'need more LeetCode' instead of naming the three language gaps: mutation, iterators, and exceptions.

## Interview follow-up

The interviewer just changed one number in the example. Interviewer: 'This function is called on a 10 GB log. What breaks, and what do you change?' Outline: name the materializing comprehension, switch to a generator or line iterator, say why `dict` not list for the lookup, and mention a test for a truncated last line. Follow-up: 'What does your type hint guarantee?' Answer: it documents intent; runtime still needs a check or a pydantic model if this is an API.

## What you would cut

Ship the smallest version of this example that still teaches the mechanism. Cut IDE autocomplete for the ten exercises, the sixth rewrite of the same two-sum, and any solution you cannot explain without the tab. Keep one timed set, the error log (pattern, edge, complexity, bug), and a re-solve date.

# exercises_a.py -- text basics (exercises 1-3)
import heapq
import re
from typing import Callable, Hashable, Iterable, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")

_WORD = re.compile(r"[a-z0-9]+(?:'[a-z]+)*")


def tokenize(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """1. Lowercase, drop punctuation, keep inner apostrophes (don't -> don't)."""
    return _WORD.findall(text.lower())


def top_k_words(text: str, k: int) -> list[tuple[str, int]]:
    """2. k most frequent words; ties broken alphabetically (deterministic)."""
    if k <= 0:
        return []
    counts: dict[str, int] = {}
    for w in tokenize(text):
        counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
    # nsmallest on (-count, word) is O(n log k) instead of sorting all n.
    best = heapq.nsmallest(k, ((-c, w) for w, c in counts.items()))
    return [(w, -c) for c, w in best]


def dedupe(items: Iterable[T], key: Callable[[T], Hashable] | None = None) -> list[T]:
    """3. Remove duplicates, keep first occurrence, preserve order."""
    seen: set[Hashable] = set()
    out: list[T] = []
    for item in items:
        k = key(item) if key else item
        if k not in seen:
            seen.add(k)
            out.append(item)
    return out


def test_a() -> None:
    assert tokenize("Hello, World! Don't panic: 3 times.") == ["hello", "world", "don't", "panic", "3", "times"]
    assert tokenize("") == [] and tokenize("!!!") == []
    text = "the cat and the hat and the bat"
    assert top_k_words(text, 2) == [("the", 3), ("and", 2)]
    assert top_k_words(text, 0) == []
    assert top_k_words("b a", 5) == [("a", 1), ("b", 1)]  # tie -> alphabetical, k > unique
    assert dedupe([3, 1, 3, 2, 1]) == [3, 1, 2]
    docs = [{"id": 1, "t": "a"}, {"id": 1, "t": "b"}, {"id": 2, "t": "c"}]
    assert dedupe(docs, key=lambda d: d["id"]) == [docs[0], docs[2]]  # dicts are unhashable, so use key=
    assert dedupe([]) == []

# run_all.py -- save the four files as exercises_a.py ... exercises_d.py, then run: python run_all.py
import importlib
import time

for name, test in [("exercises_a", "test_a"), ("exercises_b", "test_b"),
                   ("exercises_c", "test_c"), ("exercises_d", "test_d")]:
    module = importlib.import_module(name)
    started = time.perf_counter()
    getattr(module, test)()
    print(f"{name}: ok in {(time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000:.1f} ms")

Answer each aloud, closed-book, in 60 to 90 seconds, then check against the model answer. Where a line says "Evidence", use your own project if you have one; if you have not built it, say so plainly and explain how you would validate it.

## Q1. Explain list vs tuple vs set vs dict and the complexity of common operations

- **Define:** A list is a mutable ordered sequence, a tuple is an immutable ordered sequence, a set is an unordered collection of unique hashable items, and a dict maps unique hashable keys to values with insertion order preserved.
- **Mechanism:** List and tuple are arrays of references, so indexing is O(1) but searching is O(n). Set and dict are hash tables: they hash the key to find a slot, so membership, insert and delete are O(1) on average. List append is amortised O(1) because the array over-allocates; `insert(0, x)` and `pop(0)` are O(n) because everything shifts.
- **Decision:** Use a set for membership and dedupe, a dict for lookup, counting and grouping, a list when order and duplicates matter, a tuple for fixed records and dict keys, and a `deque` for queues.
- **Trade-off:** Hash tables spend memory (they keep spare slots) and need hashable keys; lists are compact and cache friendly but slow to search. A set loses duplicates and (for practical purposes) order.
- **Evidence:** "In my retrieval code I converted the list of already-seen chunk ids to a set, which turned a nested loop into a single pass." If you have no such example, say what benchmark you would run: `timeit` on 100,000 lookups in a list versus a set.

**Failure mode to mention:** `x in list` inside a loop is a hidden O(n squared); average-case O(1) for hashing is not a worst-case guarantee.

**60-90 second version:** "A list is a mutable ordered array: index is O(1), `in` is O(n), append is amortised O(1), inserting at the front is O(n). A tuple is the immutable version, which makes it hashable if its items are, so it can be a dict key. A set and a dict are hash tables: add, remove and membership are O(1) on average, a dict adds a value and keeps insertion order. I pick a set to dedupe or test membership, a dict to count or group, and a deque if I pop from the front. The cost is memory and the need for hashable keys. The classic mistake is `if x in my_list` inside a loop, which makes the whole thing quadratic."

**Follow-ups:**
- *Why is a list append amortised O(1)?* The array grows geometrically, so the rare O(n) copy is spread across many appends.
- *Can a dict key be a tuple?* Yes, if every element is hashable; a tuple holding a list is not.
- *How does a dict keep order?* Since 3.7 it stores entries in an insertion-ordered array and uses a separate index table for the hash lookup.

## Q2. What is the mutable default argument bug?

- **Define:** Default values are evaluated once at function definition, so a mutable default is shared by every call that does not pass that argument.
- **Mechanism:** `def f(x, acc=[])` creates one list object stored on the function; each call that omits `acc` appends to the same list.
- **Decision:** Default to `None` and create the list inside. A shared default is only acceptable as a deliberate memo, and then it deserves a comment.
- **Trade-off:** The `None` sentinel costs one line. If `None` is itself a legal value, use a private `_MISSING = object()` sentinel.
- **Evidence:** Mention a lint rule (for example flake8-bugbear B006) or a test that calls the function twice and checks that results do not leak between calls.

**Failure mode to mention:** state leaking across requests in a long-running server, which shows up as data from one user appearing in another's result.

**60-90 second version:** "Python evaluates default arguments once, when the function is defined. If the default is a list or dict, all calls share it, so appends accumulate across calls. I use `None` as the default and build a fresh list inside the function. In a web service this bug is nasty because the process lives for days, so one request's data can leak into the next. I would catch it with a linter rule and a test that calls the function twice."

**Follow-ups:** *What is the closure variant?* Lambdas in a loop capture the variable, not the value; bind with a default argument. *When is a mutable default fine?* A deliberate cache, clearly commented.

## Q3. Generators versus lists: when do you use each?

- **Define:** A generator produces values lazily one at a time and can be consumed once; a list stores all values in memory and can be reused.
- **Mechanism:** A function with `yield` returns a generator object that keeps its local state between `next()` calls. A generator expression is the compact form.
- **Decision:** Generator for large, streamed or early-exit data (file lines, batches for an embedding API, token streams). List when you need `len`, indexing, sorting or several passes.
- **Trade-off:** Memory and time-to-first-item versus reusability and debuggability; you cannot slice or re-iterate a generator and exceptions appear at consumption time.
- **Evidence:** "I batch documents through a generator so only one batch of vectors is in memory." If you have not done this, describe how you would measure peak memory with `tracemalloc` on a million items.

**Failure mode to mention:** silently consuming a generator twice; the second pass is empty and no error is raised.

**60-90 second version:** "A list materialises everything; a generator yields one item at a time and is single pass. I use generators when data is large or arrives as a stream, like reading a big file or batching documents to an embedding API, and when the consumer may stop early. I use a list when I need the length, random access or several passes. The trap is that a generator is exhausted after one iteration, and validation inside a generator body runs only when someone starts iterating."

**Follow-ups:** *What does `yield from` do?* Delegates to a sub-iterator. *How do async generators relate?* `async def` with `yield` produces an async generator consumed by `async for`, which is how streaming model responses are usually exposed.

## Q4. What does hashable mean, and why can't a list be a dict key?

- **Define:** An object is hashable if it has a `__hash__` that stays constant for its lifetime and an `__eq__` consistent with it (equal objects must hash equal).
- **Mechanism:** A dict stores the key at a slot picked from its hash. If the key mutated, its hash would change and the dict could no longer find it. So mutable containers (list, dict, set) set `__hash__` to `None`.
- **Decision:** Use tuples, strings, numbers, frozensets or frozen dataclasses as keys. To key by a list's content, convert it to a tuple.
- **Trade-off:** Immutability makes keys safe but means you build a new object to change one.
- **Evidence:** A test asserting `hash(obj)` works and that two equal records collide into one dict entry.

**Failure mode to mention:** a custom class that defines `__eq__` but not `__hash__` becomes unhashable; one that is mutable but hashable by identity gives surprising lookups.

**60-90 second version:** "Hashable means the object has a stable hash and equality consistent with it. Dicts and sets locate items by hash, so a key that could change after insertion would become unreachable. Lists, dicts and sets are mutable, so they are unhashable; tuples of hashables, strings, numbers and frozen dataclasses are fine. If I need a list as a key I convert to a tuple."

**Follow-ups:** *Is a tuple containing a list hashable?* No. *What does `frozen=True` on a dataclass do?* Blocks attribute assignment and generates `__hash__`.

## Q5. Dataclass versus dict versus pydantic model

- **Define:** A dict is an untyped key-value map; a dataclass is a class with typed fields and generated boilerplate; a pydantic model is a class that validates and coerces data at runtime.
- **Mechanism:** Dataclasses generate `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` from annotations but do not check types. Pydantic validates on construction and can serialise to JSON.
- **Decision:** Pydantic at the boundary where untrusted data enters (API request, model output). Dataclasses or plain classes for internal values. Dicts for genuinely dynamic shapes.
- **Trade-off:** Validation costs CPU and a dependency; dicts are fastest to write but typos become runtime `KeyError`s far from the cause.
- **Evidence:** A test that a malformed model reply raises a validation error, and a type checker run (`mypy` or `pyright`) in CI.

**Failure mode to mention:** assuming type hints on a dataclass are enforced; `Hit(doc_id=5, score="high")` constructs happily.

**60-90 second version:** "I use dicts at the edges, but as soon as data enters my code I convert it to a typed object. For untrusted input like an API body or an LLM reply I use pydantic because it validates. Inside the service I use dataclasses, frozen when the value should not change, because I get named fields, a readable repr and equality for free. The common misconception is that dataclass annotations are checked at runtime; they are not."

**Follow-ups:** *Why `frozen=True`?* Immutability and hashability. *`slots=True`?* Lower memory and no stray attributes.

## Q6. How do you design exceptions in a small library?

- **Define:** Exception design is choosing which errors you raise, what type carries the meaning, and who is expected to handle them.
- **Mechanism:** Subclass a sensible built-in (`ValueError`) for your domain error, raise with context using `raise X from e`, and catch only what you can act on.
- **Decision:** One small base class per package, separate classes when callers must react differently (retryable versus permanent).
- **Trade-off:** More classes mean a bigger API surface; too few forces callers to parse messages.
- **Evidence:** Tests with `pytest.raises` for each error path, including the retry decorator not retrying a permanent error.

**Failure mode to mention:** `except Exception: pass`, which hides real bugs, or a retry wrapper that retries on every exception including programmer errors.

**60-90 second version:** "I define a small hierarchy rooted in a base exception for the package, subclassing built-ins where it fits, such as a `ModelOutputError` that extends `ValueError`. I separate errors the caller can retry from those they cannot, chain causes with `from`, and never swallow broad exceptions. Cleanup goes in `finally` or a context manager. I test each failure path with `pytest.raises`."

**Follow-ups:** *Why `from e`?* Keeps the original traceback as `__cause__`. *Where do you catch at the top level?* At the request or job boundary, to log and return a structured error.

## Q7 (added). Write a function to chunk tokens with overlap. What do you check?

- **Define:** Chunking splits a token list into windows of fixed size where consecutive windows share `overlap` tokens.
- **Mechanism:** The step is `size - overlap`; start indices are 0, step, 2 times step, and the loop stops after a window reaches the end.
- **Decision:** Validate that `size > 0` and `0 <= overlap < size` (otherwise the step is zero or negative and the loop never ends); handle an empty or short input.
- **Trade-off:** More overlap improves recall for facts near boundaries but multiplies stored chunks and embedding cost; with size 500 and overlap 100 you store about 25% more tokens than with no overlap.
- **Evidence:** A trace of 10 tokens, size 4, overlap 1 giving three windows, written before the code.

**Failure mode to mention:** an infinite loop when `overlap >= size`, or a final window that duplicates the previous one.

**60-90 second version:** "Step equals size minus overlap. I loop over start indices by that step, slice size tokens, and stop once a window reaches the end so I do not emit a duplicate tail. I reject non-positive sizes and overlaps that are not smaller than size, and return an empty list for empty input. I would test with ten tokens, size four, overlap one, which must give three windows."

**Follow-ups:** *How would you chunk by sentences?* Split on boundaries then pack sentences up to the token limit. *Why count tokens, not characters?* Model limits and cost are in tokens.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Interview tab: a spoken-answer failure, the actual next question, and the essay you would not say out loud. In a 35-minute screen the candidate wrote a correct-looking group-by on a list of events, then froze when asked the complexity of `list.pop(0)` and why a `set` membership test was in the inner loop. They had practised only with autocomplete. The function mutated a default-argument dict, so a second call leaked keys from the first. They could not write a 4-line test for the empty input. The review notes said 'need more LeetCode' instead of naming the three language gaps: mutation, iterators, and exceptions.

## Interview follow-up

You already gave a 90-second answer; this is the probe. Interviewer: 'This function is called on a 10 GB log. What breaks, and what do you change?' Outline: name the materializing comprehension, switch to a generator or line iterator, say why `dict` not list for the lookup, and mention a test for a truncated last line. Follow-up: 'What does your type hint guarantee?' Answer: it documents intent; runtime still needs a check or a pydantic model if this is an API.

## What you would cut

Say less: keep define, mechanism, decision, trade-off, evidence. Cut IDE autocomplete for the ten exercises, the sixth rewrite of the same two-sum, and any solution you cannot explain without the tab. Keep one timed set, the error log (pattern, edge, complexity, bug), and a re-solve date.

lessons.summary: Build and explain a small FastAPI service in front of a model: async I/O, timeouts, retries with backoff, offline tests, SSE streaming and production API hygiene.
keyPoints: Async helps with many concurrent I/O waits such as model calls; it does not speed up CPU-bound work and a blocking call stalls the whole loop.
Use per-attempt timeouts plus a total deadline; retry only timeouts, 429 and 5xx with exponential backoff and jitter, honouring Retry-After.
Retry at one layer only: nested retries multiply load (3 layers of 3 tries is 27 calls).
Put the model behind an interface and test with a scripted fake; mock the client, integration-test the adapter sparingly, eval quality separately.
Streaming responses fix the status at 200, so report mid-stream errors in-band and close the upstream stream in a shielded finally on disconnect.
Validate with pydantic at the boundary, inject collaborators with Depends, authenticate and authorise on every request, return one stable error shape.
Never log prompts, completions or keys by default; log request id, latency, token counts and retry counts.

check.q: Twenty independent model calls each take about 2 seconds. You run them with asyncio.gather under a Semaphore(5). Roughly how long does the batch take?
options: About 2 seconds
About 8 seconds
About 40 seconds
About 10 seconds
check.why: Five calls run at a time, so 20 calls take four waves of about 2 seconds each, roughly 8 seconds. Unbounded gather would be about 2 seconds but may hit rate limits; sequential would be about 40.

check.q: A model API returns HTTP 400 for a malformed request. What should your retry helper do?
options: Retry with exponential backoff up to four times
Retry once after reading Retry-After
Raise immediately because retrying cannot fix a bad request
Switch to streaming mode and retry
check.why: 400-level errors other than 429 mean the request itself is wrong, so retrying wastes time and money. Retry timeouts, connection errors, 429 and 5xx; fail fast on permanent errors.

check.q: A client disconnects mid-stream from your SSE endpoint. What is the key thing your server code must ensure?
options: Return a 499 status code to the client
Retry the whole request automatically
Buffer the remaining tokens for later replay
Cancel generation by closing the upstream stream in a finally block that is shielded from cancellation
check.why: Starlette cancels the response task on disconnect. Cleanup in finally, shielded so the await is not itself cancelled, closes the upstream stream so you stop generating and paying for unread tokens. The status was already sent.
